name: .NET
shortDescription: The cross-platform runtime, SDK, libraries, and tooling behind modern C# applications.
overview: .NET is a free, open-source developer platform for building web, cloud, desktop, mobile, data, and background applications.
detail: Think of .NET as a complete execution and development environment: the SDK compiles and packages applications, the runtime executes managed code, base libraries provide common capabilities, and tooling supports testing, diagnostics, publishing, and deployment across operating systems.

concepts.title: Runtime and CLR
concepts.description: Executes managed code and provides garbage collection, type safety, exceptions, and just-in-time compilation.

concepts.title: SDK and CLI
concepts.description: Creates, restores, builds, tests, publishes, and manages projects through consistent dotnet commands.

concepts.title: Base class libraries
concepts.description: Reusable APIs for collections, networking, files, JSON, concurrency, cryptography, and more.

concepts.title: NuGet ecosystem
concepts.description: A package system for sharing versioned libraries and restoring repeatable dependency graphs.

architecture.description: Source code is compiled into intermediate language and metadata, then loaded by the runtime and executed as native instructions.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A modern console application can use top-level statements, dependency-aware configuration, and async APIs without ceremony.

bestPractices: Pin the target framework and centralize package versions for predictable builds.
Use nullable reference types and analyzers to catch defects before runtime.
Publish with the deployment model—framework-dependent, self-contained, or container—that matches operations.
Measure with built-in diagnostics before attempting performance optimizations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the .NET SDK and runtime?
interviewQuestions.answer: The runtime executes compiled applications. The SDK includes the runtime plus compilers, templates, build tooling, and commands needed to create and publish them.

interviewQuestions.question: What does managed code mean?
interviewQuestions.answer: Managed code runs under the CLR, which supplies services such as memory management, type safety, exception handling, and runtime compilation.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose a self-contained deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Choose it when the target should not depend on a separately installed runtime and the larger artifact and patching responsibility are acceptable.

note: The runtime, SDK, and target framework are related but distinct. Record all three when diagnosing build or deployment differences.
tip: Keep a global.json when a repository depends on a specific SDK feature or build behavior.
warning: Do not assume a successful local build proves the published artifact will run on a different OS or CPU architecture.

name: C#
shortDescription: A strongly typed, expressive language for object-oriented, functional, and asynchronous programming.
overview: C# is a modern, statically typed language designed for productive application development across the .NET platform.
detail: C# combines a rich type system with approachable syntax. Its records, pattern matching, LINQ, generics, asynchronous programming model, and nullable analysis help teams express domain rules clearly while retaining strong compile-time checks.

concepts.title: Type system
concepts.description: Value and reference types, generics, nullability, and inference make contracts explicit without excessive syntax.

concepts.title: Async and tasks
concepts.description: async and await express non-blocking I/O as readable control flow while Task represents future completion.

concepts.title: LINQ
concepts.description: Composable query operators transform in-memory data and provider-backed query expressions.

concepts.title: Records and patterns
concepts.description: Records model value-like data while patterns make branching over shapes and values concise.

architecture.description: Language features help move data from boundary contracts through domain behavior to infrastructure without losing type information.

code.label: Order.cs
code.introduction: Records and property patterns create compact, immutable contracts and readable business decisions.

bestPractices: Enable nullable reference types and fix warnings at boundaries.
Prefer small immutable types for messages and values that should not change.
Use async all the way for I/O-bound work and pass cancellation tokens.
Keep LINQ queries readable; name intermediate results when intent becomes hidden.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a class and a record?
interviewQuestions.answer: Classes use reference identity by default. Records emphasize value equality and concise immutable-style construction, though both remain reference types unless record struct is used.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should async void usually be avoided?
interviewQuestions.answer: It cannot be awaited, composes poorly, and propagates exceptions differently. It is generally reserved for event handlers.

interviewQuestions.question: What does deferred execution mean in LINQ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Many LINQ operators describe a query that runs only when enumerated, so data and side effects may be evaluated later or more than once.

note: Concise syntax should expose intent. If a clever expression makes debugging or ownership harder, a named method is usually better.
tip: Model domain values such as Money or Email as focused types instead of passing primitive strings and decimals everywhere.
warning: Avoid blocking Task results with .Result or .Wait() in request paths; this can reduce throughput and create deadlock risks in some contexts.

name: Dependency Injection
shortDescription: Compose applications from explicit, testable services with managed lifetimes and clear boundaries.
overview: Dependency injection separates service construction from service use, making dependencies explicit and application composition centralized.
detail: The built-in .NET container resolves constructor dependencies from registrations at the composition root. Lifetimes describe ownership: singleton for application-wide instances, scoped for one logical operation such as a web request, and transient for a new instance per resolution.

concepts.title: Composition root
concepts.description: The startup location where concrete services, interfaces, configuration, and decorators are assembled.

concepts.title: Service lifetimes
concepts.description: Singleton, scoped, and transient registrations define instance reuse and disposal boundaries.

concepts.title: Constructor injection
concepts.description: Required collaborators appear in the constructor, producing explicit and testable object contracts.

concepts.title: Options pattern
concepts.description: Typed configuration objects separate configuration binding and validation from service behavior.

architecture.description: The container builds an object graph at the composition root and supplies dependencies to application entry points.

code.label: DependencyInjection.cs
code.introduction: Group registrations by feature and validate configuration when the application starts.

bestPractices: Register services near their feature and keep the composition root readable.
Inject abstractions at real boundaries, not an interface for every class.
Validate options on startup so invalid configuration fails fast.
Match a dependency's lifetime to the lifetime of everything it captures.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a captive dependency?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when a longer-lived service, commonly a singleton, captures a shorter-lived dependency such as a scoped service and unintentionally extends its lifetime.

interviewQuestions.question: When should a service be transient?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use transient for lightweight, stateless services that can be created per resolution and do not need shared operation state.

interviewQuestions.question: Is dependency injection the same as the dependency inversion principle?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. DI is a composition technique; dependency inversion is a design principle about high-level policy depending on abstractions rather than low-level details.

note: The container is an application assembly mechanism, not a global service locator to call from domain code.
tip: Enable service-provider validation in development to catch invalid lifetime graphs early.
warning: Do not inject scoped services into singletons unless you create and dispose an explicit scope for a well-defined operation.

name: ASP.NET Core
shortDescription: A high-performance, cross-platform framework for APIs, web apps, real-time systems, and services.
overview: ASP.NET Core is the web framework for building HTTP APIs, server-rendered applications, real-time endpoints, and cloud services on .NET.
detail: Requests enter Kestrel, pass through an ordered middleware pipeline, and reach an endpoint selected by routing. Built-in facilities cover configuration, logging, dependency injection, authentication, authorization, health checks, caching, and graceful shutdown.

concepts.title: Middleware pipeline
concepts.description: Ordered components inspect, short-circuit, or pass HTTP requests and responses through the application.

concepts.title: Routing and endpoints
concepts.description: Routes match requests to controllers, Razor pages, hubs, health checks, or minimal API handlers.

concepts.title: Hosting model
concepts.description: WebApplication coordinates configuration, services, logging, server startup, and application lifetime.

concepts.title: Cross-cutting services
concepts.description: Authentication, problem details, rate limits, output caching, and telemetry integrate at the platform level.

architecture.description: The request pipeline applies cross-cutting policy before dispatching to an endpoint that coordinates application and infrastructure services.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A focused API configures platform services first, then composes middleware in an intentional order.

bestPractices: Keep middleware order explicit and cover security-sensitive ordering with integration tests.
Return consistent problem details for failures instead of ad hoc error shapes.
Propagate request cancellation to database and outbound HTTP operations.
Expose separate liveness and readiness checks when orchestration depends on them.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does middleware order matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each middleware wraps the next component. Ordering changes which requests it sees and whether authentication, authorization, exceptions, and endpoints behave correctly.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Kestrel?
interviewQuestions.answer: Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's cross-platform web server. It can be internet-facing or run behind a reverse proxy depending on the deployment.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose controllers over minimal APIs?
interviewQuestions.answer: Controllers are useful when conventions, filters, model-binding customization, and a structured large API surface outweigh minimal APIs' compact vertical-slice style.

note: Treat the HTTP layer as an adapter. Business rules should remain testable without constructing HTTP contexts.
tip: Use WebApplicationFactory integration tests to verify routing, filters, serialization, authentication, and middleware together.
warning: A health endpoint that always returns success can cause an orchestrator to route traffic to an application that cannot serve real requests.

name: Entity Framework Core
shortDescription: An object-relational mapper for expressive data access, change tracking, migrations, and transactions.
overview: Entity Framework Core is a lightweight, extensible ORM that maps .NET models and LINQ queries to database operations.
detail: A DbContext represents a unit of work over mapped entities. Providers translate expression trees into database queries, change tracking detects mutations, and migrations describe schema evolution. Good EF Core use still requires database literacy and query inspection.

concepts.title: DbContext
concepts.description: A short-lived unit of work that coordinates queries, tracked changes, transactions, and persistence.

concepts.title: Query translation
concepts.description: LINQ expression trees are translated by a provider into database-specific commands.

concepts.title: Change tracking
concepts.description: Tracked entity state determines which inserts, updates, and deletes SaveChanges will issue.

concepts.title: Migrations
concepts.description: Versioned schema operations let teams review and deploy database changes deliberately.

architecture.description: Application queries pass through a DbContext and provider, which translates operations for the target relational database.

code.label: OrderQueries.cs
code.introduction: Project read models at the database, disable tracking when updating is unnecessary, and make cancellation explicit.

bestPractices: Project only the columns required for read models.
Use AsNoTracking for read-only queries and bounded result sets for lists.
Inspect generated SQL and query plans for important paths.
Review migrations as production code and separate migration execution from application startup when needed.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the recommended DbContext lifetime in a web app?
interviewQuestions.answer: Scoped is the common default, aligning one context with one request or unit of work. It is not thread-safe and should not be shared across concurrent operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What causes the N+1 query problem?
interviewQuestions.answer: Code loads a set of parent rows and then triggers an additional query per row for related data, often through repeated explicit or lazy loading.

interviewQuestions.question: When should AsNoTracking be used?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it when entities are read-only in the current unit of work; it avoids change-tracking overhead.

note: LINQ is an abstraction over a provider. A query that is cheap in memory may translate into expensive SQL.
tip: Tag important queries and capture their generated SQL during performance investigations.
warning: Do not hold a DbContext for the lifetime of an application or use the same instance from concurrent threads.

name: Blazor
shortDescription: Build interactive web interfaces with Razor components, C#, and flexible server or client rendering modes.
overview: Blazor is a component-based web UI framework that lets .NET developers build interactive experiences with C# and Razor.
detail: Razor components combine markup and C# state. Applications can render static HTML, run interactivity on the server, execute .NET in WebAssembly, or choose rendering per component. The right mode depends on startup, latency, offline, security, and hosting needs.

concepts.title: Razor components
concepts.description: Reusable UI units combine parameters, markup, event handlers, state, and lifecycle methods.

concepts.title: Render modes
concepts.description: Static, interactive server, interactive WebAssembly, and auto modes trade startup cost, latency, and hosting needs.

concepts.title: Component lifecycle
concepts.description: Lifecycle methods coordinate initialization, parameter changes, rendering, and browser interop.

concepts.title: State and forms
concepts.description: Binding, cascading values, EditForm, validation, and scoped services manage user interactions.

architecture.description: A Razor component renders UI and handles events through either a server circuit or a WebAssembly runtime before calling application services.

code.label: Counter.razor
code.introduction: A component keeps its state close to its markup and exposes a small, accessible interaction surface.

bestPractices: Choose render mode per user experience and operational constraints.
Keep components focused; move business behavior into injected application services.
Use stable keys for dynamic lists and cancel work when components are disposed.
Design loading, reconnecting, empty, and failure states as first-class UI.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Server and WebAssembly interactivity differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: Server interactivity executes components on the server over a real-time circuit; WebAssembly downloads a .NET runtime and executes components in the browser.

interviewQuestions.question: What triggers a component render?
interviewQuestions.answer: Parameter updates, handled events, and explicit StateHasChanged calls can schedule rendering. The renderer then applies a diff to the DOM.

interviewQuestions.question: When is JavaScript interop appropriate?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use it for browser capabilities or existing JavaScript libraries without practical .NET abstractions, keeping the boundary small and lifecycle-aware.

note: Rendering and interactivity are separate decisions. A page may be server-rendered without becoming an interactive server component.
tip: Test the reconnect and slow-network experience when using interactive server rendering.
warning: Never place trusted secrets in WebAssembly code or browser-delivered configuration; users can inspect all client assets.

name: Minimal APIs
shortDescription: Create focused HTTP endpoints with compact route handlers, typed results, filters, and OpenAPI support.
overview: Minimal APIs provide a concise way to define HTTP endpoints while retaining ASP.NET Core's hosting, dependency injection, security, and diagnostics.
detail: Route handlers bind input from routes, queries, headers, bodies, services, and custom binders. Endpoint groups, filters, typed results, validation, and OpenAPI metadata support modular APIs without requiring controller classes.

concepts.title: Route handlers
concepts.description: Delegates receive bound request values and services, then return serializable or typed HTTP results.

concepts.title: Route groups
concepts.description: Groups share prefixes, metadata, filters, authorization, and naming conventions.

concepts.title: Typed results
concepts.description: Concrete result types improve compile-time contracts, tests, and OpenAPI description.

concepts.title: Endpoint filters
concepts.description: Filters wrap selected handlers for validation, logging, policy, or other endpoint-level behavior.

architecture.description: An endpoint group applies shared HTTP policy, binds a request contract, calls an application use case, and maps the outcome to typed results.

code.label: OrderEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: Group related endpoints and make the success and failure contract visible in the handler signature.

bestPractices: Group endpoints by cohesive capability, not by HTTP verb.
Use request and response contracts rather than exposing persistence entities.
Give endpoints stable names and include useful OpenAPI metadata.
Keep handlers thin by delegating workflow and business policy to application services.

interviewQuestions.question: Are minimal APIs only for small applications?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. They can scale when endpoints are organized by feature and handlers delegate complexity. Their suitability depends more on conventions and team structure than raw endpoint count.

interviewQuestions.question: How are services injected into a route handler?
interviewQuestions.answer: Registered services are resolved from dependency injection through inferred or explicit parameter binding.

interviewQuestions.question: What do typed results improve?
interviewQuestions.answer: They provide concrete response types that help compile-time checking, endpoint tests, and generated OpenAPI metadata.

note: Minimal syntax does not mean minimal design. Contracts, validation, security, observability, and failure semantics still matter.
tip: Use route groups as the module boundary for shared authorization and filters.
warning: Avoid returning database entities directly; accidental navigation properties or schema changes can leak into the API contract.

name: Authentication & Authorization
shortDescription: Establish identity, enforce policy, protect credentials, and design secure application boundaries.
overview: Authentication establishes who a principal is; authorization decides what that principal may do in a specific context.
detail: ASP.NET Core authentication handlers validate credentials such as cookies or bearer tokens and construct a ClaimsPrincipal. Authorization evaluates roles, claims, policies, requirements, and resource context after authentication—ideally with deny-by-default rules.

concepts.title: Schemes and handlers
concepts.description: A scheme selects the handler that authenticates, challenges, or forbids a request.

concepts.title: Claims principal
concepts.description: One or more identities and their claims represent the authenticated caller.

concepts.title: Policy authorization
concepts.description: Named policies combine reusable requirements that handlers evaluate against user and resource.

concepts.title: Token lifecycle
concepts.description: Issuance, audience, expiry, rotation, revocation, and key management shape token safety.

architecture.description: An identity provider issues credentials; the application validates them, builds a principal, then evaluates policy before invoking a protected resource.

code.label: Authorization.cs
code.introduction: A policy expresses business permission as a named requirement instead of scattering claim checks through endpoints.

bestPractices: Validate issuer, audience, signature, lifetime, and algorithms for bearer tokens.
Prefer policy and resource-based authorization over inline role checks.
Keep signing keys and client secrets outside source control and rotate them.
Return minimal information from authentication failures and log securely with correlation.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authentication verifies identity. Authorization evaluates whether that identity is permitted to perform an action on a resource.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are refresh tokens treated differently from access tokens?
interviewQuestions.answer: Refresh tokens are longer-lived credentials used to obtain access tokens, so they require stronger storage, rotation, reuse detection, and revocation controls.

interviewQuestions.question: What is resource-based authorization?
interviewQuestions.answer: It evaluates access using both the principal and the actual resource instance—for example, whether the current user owns a document.

note: CORS is a browser cross-origin policy; it is not authentication or authorization and does not protect server-to-server calls.
tip: Write negative authorization tests—anonymous, wrong role, missing claim, wrong tenant, and non-owner—not only the happy path.
warning: Do not decode a JWT and trust its claims without cryptographically validating the token and its intended issuer and audience.

name: Azure for .NET
shortDescription: Run, integrate, observe, and secure .NET workloads using Azure-managed services and identity.
overview: Azure offers managed compute, data, messaging, identity, secrets, and observability services that integrate naturally with .NET.
detail: A sound Azure design begins with workload requirements rather than a service catalog. Choose compute based on execution and scaling needs, prefer managed identity over stored credentials, design transient-failure handling, and make telemetry, cost, network boundaries, and deployment part of the architecture.

concepts.title: Managed compute
concepts.description: App Service, Container Apps, Functions, and Kubernetes offer different control, scaling, and operational trade-offs.

concepts.title: Managed identity
concepts.description: Workloads obtain Entra-backed tokens for Azure resources without shipping long-lived application secrets.

concepts.title: Messaging
concepts.description: Service Bus and Event Hubs decouple workloads across commands, events, streams, retries, and backpressure.

concepts.title: Observability
concepts.description: OpenTelemetry and Azure Monitor connect traces, metrics, logs, alerts, and dependency context.

architecture.description: A managed entry point routes traffic to .NET compute, which uses identity-based access to data and messaging while emitting correlated telemetry.

code.label: AzureClient.cs
code.introduction: DefaultAzureCredential supports local developer identity and managed identity in Azure without changing application code.

bestPractices: Use managed identity and role assignments instead of embedded credentials.
Define infrastructure as code and promote the same templates through environments.
Set timeouts, retries with jitter, and circuit breaking only for transient operations.
Design telemetry, budgets, backup, recovery objectives, and region strategy before production.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Azure Container Apps over AKS?
interviewQuestions.answer: Container Apps suits teams wanting container-based scaling and revisions with less cluster operations; AKS fits workloads needing Kubernetes APIs, ecosystem control, or specialized cluster capabilities.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does managed identity solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It lets an Azure resource obtain short-lived Entra tokens for other resources without storing and rotating a client secret in the application.

interviewQuestions.question: How should transient Azure failures be handled?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use bounded retries with backoff and jitter for operations known to be safe to retry, plus timeouts, observability, and idempotency where side effects are possible.

note: Cloud-native is an operating model as much as a hosting location: automated delivery, observability, resiliency, and ownership all matter.
tip: Use the same credential abstraction locally and in Azure, but verify exactly which credential wins in each environment.
warning: Retries can amplify an outage or duplicate effects. Bound them, add jitter, and make write operations idempotent before retrying.

name: Microservices
shortDescription: Design independently deployable services around business capabilities and operational ownership.
overview: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services aligned to cohesive business capabilities and owned data.
detail: The architecture trades in-process simplicity for deployment autonomy and distributed-systems costs. Clear boundaries, independent data ownership, asynchronous messaging, observability, idempotency, and team ownership are more important than service count.

concepts.title: Service boundaries
concepts.description: Capabilities and change patterns shape cohesive services more reliably than technical layers or tables.

concepts.title: Data ownership
concepts.description: Each service controls its persistence model and shares behavior through contracts, not database joins.

concepts.title: Messaging patterns
concepts.description: Events, queues, outbox delivery, idempotent consumers, and sagas coordinate without global transactions.

concepts.title: Operational autonomy
concepts.description: Independent deployment requires health, telemetry, release safety, capacity, and clear ownership per service.

architecture.description: Clients enter through an edge; independently deployed services own their data and exchange durable messages through a broker.

code.label: IdempotentConsumer.cs
code.introduction: A consumer records message identity in the same transaction as its business change so redelivery is safe.

bestPractices: Start with boundaries and ownership; do not split solely to follow an architecture trend.
Assume messages may be delayed, duplicated, or reordered.
Use correlation identifiers and distributed tracing across synchronous and asynchronous hops.
Deploy compatibility changes before removing old contract behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a database per service recommended?
interviewQuestions.answer: It preserves autonomy and prevents other services from coupling to internal schemas. The storage can be physically shared, but ownership and access boundaries must remain clear.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: It atomically records a business change and an outgoing message in one local transaction, then publishes the message asynchronously to avoid dual-write inconsistency.

interviewQuestions.question: When is a modular monolith a better choice?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the domain or team boundaries are still evolving and independent deployment benefits do not justify distributed operations, latency, and consistency costs.

note: A service is a socio-technical boundary: code, data, deployment, telemetry, support, and a team capable of changing it.
tip: Prove modular boundaries inside a monolith before paying the operational cost of network separation.
warning: Never use synchronous retries as a substitute for designing partial failure and idempotency.

name: Clean Architecture
shortDescription: Protect business policy from delivery and infrastructure details through explicit dependency direction.
overview: Clean Architecture keeps core business rules independent from frameworks, databases, transport protocols, and user interfaces.
detail: Dependencies point inward toward stable domain and application policy. Outer adapters translate HTTP, persistence, messaging, or UI concerns. The goal is not a fixed folder count; it is replaceable details, testable use cases, and boundaries that match the system's real change pressures.

concepts.title: Dependency rule
concepts.description: Source-code dependencies point toward policies; inner layers do not reference outer implementation details.

concepts.title: Use cases
concepts.description: Application services coordinate domain behavior, authorization context, persistence ports, and outcomes.

concepts.title: Ports and adapters
concepts.description: Interfaces define required capabilities while outer adapters implement HTTP, database, or message integration.

concepts.title: Domain model
concepts.description: Entities and value objects enforce business invariants without depending on delivery frameworks.

architecture.description: External adapters depend on application ports, and application orchestration depends on the domain—not the reverse.

code.label: PlaceOrder.cs
code.introduction: A use case coordinates policy through ports without knowing whether input arrived over HTTP or where data is stored.

bestPractices: Introduce a boundary when it protects a meaningful policy or source of change.
Keep domain invariants inside domain types, not only in controllers or validators.
Name use cases in business language and return explicit outcomes.
Test architecture rules automatically if dependency direction is important.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the dependency rule?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dependencies should point inward toward higher-level policy, so domain and application code do not depend on UI, database, or framework details.

interviewQuestions.question: Does every project need four class-library projects?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Project layout is a tool. Small applications can preserve boundaries with namespaces and tests; larger systems may benefit from compile-time project separation.

interviewQuestions.question: Where should validation live?
interviewQuestions.answer: Input-shape validation belongs near the boundary; business invariants belong in the domain; use-case preconditions belong in the application layer.

note: Clean Architecture optimizes for changeability and testability, not for maximizing interfaces and folders.
tip: Start by drawing dependency arrows and ownership boundaries before choosing project names.
warning: A repository abstraction that merely mirrors every ORM method adds ceremony without protecting useful policy.

name: Design Patterns
shortDescription: A vocabulary of reusable design structures for recurring collaboration and change problems.
overview: Design patterns describe proven arrangements of responsibilities and collaborations for recurring software design problems.
detail: Patterns are communication tools, not mandatory templates. Strategy varies behavior, decorator layers responsibilities, adapter translates incompatible contracts, factory centralizes creation, and observer distributes notifications. Apply them when the variation or coupling they address is real.

concepts.title: Creational patterns
concepts.description: Factories, builders, and prototypes separate construction decisions from consumers.

concepts.title: Structural patterns
concepts.description: Adapters, decorators, composites, and facades shape how objects and systems fit together.

concepts.title: Behavioral patterns
concepts.description: Strategies, observers, commands, and mediators organize algorithms and collaboration.

concepts.title: Pattern trade-offs
concepts.description: Each pattern shifts complexity; the benefit must outweigh indirection, objects, and conventions.

architecture.description: A caller depends on a stable strategy contract while the composition root selects a behavior suited to current policy.

code.label: PricingStrategy.cs
code.introduction: Strategy replaces branching that changes for different pricing policies with a focused, selectable behavior.

bestPractices: Name the design pressure before naming a pattern.
Prefer language features and simple composition when they solve the problem clearly.
Keep pattern participants cohesive and make selection rules visible.
Document trade-offs when a pattern introduces meaningful indirection.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Strategy and State differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: They have similar structure, but Strategy selects an interchangeable algorithm while State models behavior that changes with an object's internal state transitions.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Adapter and Facade?
interviewQuestions.answer: Adapter changes an interface so a client can use it. Facade provides a simpler entry point over a subsystem without necessarily adapting an incompatible contract.

interviewQuestions.question: When is a pattern over-engineering?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the predicted variation is unlikely, the simpler design is already easy to change, or the added abstractions make ownership and behavior harder to understand.

note: Patterns give teams names for trade-offs. They do not remove the need to understand the forces in a specific design.
tip: Study a pattern beside the refactoring pressure that leads to it, not as an isolated class diagram.
warning: Do not force every class into a GoF pattern; unnecessary abstraction makes simple changes expensive.

name: Docker
shortDescription: Package .NET applications and runtime dependencies into repeatable, portable container images.
overview: Docker packages an application, its runtime, and filesystem dependencies into an immutable image executed as isolated containers.
detail: For .NET, multi-stage builds separate SDK compilation from the smaller runtime image. Containers should write state to external services or mounted volumes, receive configuration at runtime, expose health signals, and run as a non-root user where possible.

concepts.title: Images and layers
concepts.description: Immutable layers describe a filesystem and startup configuration, enabling caching and content-addressed distribution.

concepts.title: Containers
concepts.description: Running image instances isolate processes and files while sharing the host kernel.

concepts.title: Multi-stage builds
concepts.description: A build stage compiles with the SDK and a final stage carries only publish output and runtime dependencies.

concepts.title: Compose
concepts.description: A declarative local topology coordinates services, networks, volumes, environment, and health dependencies.

architecture.description: Source is compiled in an SDK stage, copied into a minimal runtime image, and executed as a replaceable container connected to external state.

code.label: Dockerfile
code.introduction: A multi-stage Dockerfile restores deterministically, publishes once, and runs the final image without root privileges.
code.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["Portal.Api.csproj", "."]
RUN dotnet restore "Portal.Api.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "Portal.Api.csproj" -c Release -o /app --no-restore

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
USER $APP_UID
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Portal.Api.dll"]

bestPractices: Use multi-stage builds and a minimal trusted runtime base image.
Copy project files before source to preserve dependency restore caching.
Run as a non-root user and scan both dependencies and the final image.
Keep secrets out of layers, build arguments, and committed Compose files.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an image and a container?
interviewQuestions.answer: An image is an immutable package definition; a container is a running instance with a writable layer and runtime configuration.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use a multi-stage build?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps compilers, source, and build caches out of the runtime image, reducing size and attack surface.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should container state be externalized?
interviewQuestions.answer: Containers are replaceable. External databases, object stores, or volumes preserve durable state across restarts, rescheduling, and scaling.

note: A successful image build proves packaging, not that the application starts correctly with real dependencies and configuration.
tip: Build from the repository root when project references or shared files live outside the API project folder.
warning: Never bake production secrets into an image; image layers remain inspectable even after a later layer removes a file.

name: Kubernetes
shortDescription: Orchestrate containerized workloads with declarative scheduling, service discovery, rollout, and recovery.
overview: Kubernetes continuously reconciles declared workload state with running containers across a cluster.
detail: Pods run one or more tightly coupled containers; Deployments manage replicas and rollout; Services provide stable discovery; Ingress or Gateway resources route external traffic; probes communicate lifecycle; and configuration is injected separately from images.

concepts.title: Desired state
concepts.description: Controllers watch resources and repeatedly reconcile observed state toward the declared specification.

concepts.title: Pods and deployments
concepts.description: Pods are scheduling units; Deployments manage replica sets, updates, rollback, and availability.

concepts.title: Services and ingress
concepts.description: Services provide stable internal discovery while ingress or gateways expose controlled external routes.

concepts.title: Probes and resources
concepts.description: Startup, readiness, liveness, requests, and limits inform safe scheduling and traffic decisions.

architecture.description: External traffic enters a gateway and Service, which selects ready .NET pods managed by a Deployment and connected to managed state.

code.label: deployment.yaml
code.introduction: Readiness controls traffic while liveness detects a stuck process; resource requests give the scheduler useful information.
code.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/orders-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }

bestPractices: Set realistic resource requests using observed workload data.
Use separate startup, readiness, and liveness semantics.
Deploy immutable image tags or digests and record configuration provenance.
Plan disruption budgets, graceful shutdown, rollout safety, and rollback together.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between readiness and liveness probes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Readiness decides whether a pod should receive traffic. Liveness decides whether Kubernetes should restart the container.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a Kubernetes Service provide?
interviewQuestions.answer: It gives a stable virtual address and discovery name over a changing set of selected pods.

interviewQuestions.question: Why set resource requests?
interviewQuestions.answer: The scheduler uses requests to place pods, and autoscaling or capacity decisions depend on having meaningful resource expectations.

note: Kubernetes automates declared operations; it does not make an application stateless, resilient, or observable by itself.
tip: Make the application stop accepting new work before termination and finish in-flight requests within the grace period.
warning: A liveness probe that depends on a downstream database can restart every healthy app instance during a database outage.

name: Testing
shortDescription: Build confidence through focused unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end feedback loops.
overview: Testing provides layered evidence that units, integrations, contracts, and complete user flows behave as intended.
detail: Fast unit tests protect deterministic policy; integration tests verify database, HTTP pipeline, serialization, or broker behavior; contract tests protect service compatibility; and a small number of end-to-end tests cover critical journeys. Test shape should follow risk, not a fixed pyramid quota.

concepts.title: Unit tests
concepts.description: Fast, isolated checks of deterministic behavior and edge cases without infrastructure.

concepts.title: Integration tests
concepts.description: Verify real boundaries such as database providers, HTTP middleware, serialization, and authentication.

concepts.title: Contract tests
concepts.description: Assert that producer and consumer expectations remain compatible as services evolve.

concepts.title: End-to-end tests
concepts.description: Exercise a small set of critical user outcomes through the deployed surface.

architecture.description: A balanced suite gives broad, fast domain feedback and progressively narrower but higher-fidelity checks at system boundaries.

code.label: OrderTests.cs
code.introduction: A useful test names the behavior, arranges only relevant state, and asserts an externally meaningful outcome.

bestPractices: Name tests after observable behavior, condition, and outcome.
Use real infrastructure in integration tests when provider behavior matters.
Control time, identifiers, and randomness through explicit seams.
Keep tests independent and make failure output reveal the violated behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: What should be mocked?
interviewQuestions.answer: Mock narrow outbound boundaries when controlling behavior is valuable. Avoid mocking the object under test, data structures, or every internal collaborator.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the value of an integration test?
interviewQuestions.answer: It exposes false assumptions about real frameworks and infrastructure—translation, configuration, serialization, transactions, routing, and security.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you prevent flaky tests?
interviewQuestions.answer: Remove uncontrolled time and concurrency, isolate data, await asynchronous completion, avoid shared mutable state, and capture diagnostic evidence.

note: Coverage is a map of executed code, not proof that the right behaviors and failure cases were asserted.
tip: Write a regression test that fails for the reported defect before changing production code.
warning: An in-memory database substitute may not reproduce relational constraints, transactions, collation, or SQL translation.

name: Performance
shortDescription: Measure latency, throughput, allocation, and saturation before optimizing the system bottleneck.
overview: Performance engineering turns user and capacity goals into measurable budgets, diagnoses bottlenecks, and validates improvements under realistic load.
detail: The most valuable optimizations usually reduce expensive I/O, unnecessary work, payload size, contention, and allocation in hot paths. Metrics, traces, profilers, load tests, and representative data show where time is spent and whether a change improves end-to-end outcomes.

concepts.title: Latency and percentiles
concepts.description: Median describes typical response while tail percentiles reveal slow experiences hidden by averages.

concepts.title: Throughput and saturation
concepts.description: Work per interval must be understood beside queues, CPU, memory, connections, and dependency capacity.

concepts.title: Allocation and GC
concepts.description: Allocation rate and object lifetime influence collection frequency, pauses, and memory footprint.

concepts.title: Measurement
concepts.description: Benchmarks isolate code; load tests evaluate systems; profiles locate time and allocation in realistic paths.

architecture.description: A request budget is consumed across edge, application, cache, database, and network calls, all observed through correlated telemetry.

code.label: ProductCache.cs
code.introduction: Cache-aside can remove repeated I/O, but the cache must be bounded, observable, and allowed to miss safely.

bestPractices: Define performance budgets and representative workloads before optimization.
Inspect database queries and downstream calls before micro-optimizing C#.
Track percentiles, error rate, throughput, saturation, and allocation together.
Benchmark release builds and prevent dead-code elimination or unrealistic inputs.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are percentiles better than average latency alone?
interviewQuestions.answer: Averages hide the distribution. P95 or P99 reveal tail experiences that often dominate timeouts and user dissatisfaction.

interviewQuestions.question: When can caching make a system worse?
interviewQuestions.answer: It adds invalidation, staleness, memory, stampede, and consistency concerns; low reuse or oversized keys can cost more than the saved work.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a benchmark and a load test?
interviewQuestions.answer: A benchmark isolates a code path under controlled conditions. A load test exercises a system under concurrency and dependency constraints.

note: Optimize the constraint that limits the user or capacity objective, not the code that merely looks inefficient.
tip: Capture a trace for a slow request and follow the critical path before opening a microbenchmark project.
warning: Unbounded caches and queues can convert a latency problem into memory exhaustion during sustained load.

name: Interview Questions
shortDescription: Practice explaining .NET decisions, trade-offs, failure modes, and production reasoning with clarity.
overview: Strong .NET interview answers connect a clear concept to a concrete example, trade-off, failure mode, and verification method.
detail: Interview preparation is more durable when organized around reasoning rather than memorized definitions. Explain the mechanism, state when it helps, identify costs, describe how it fails, and connect the answer to evidence from a project you have actually built or operated.

concepts.title: Concept
concepts.description: Start with a precise definition in plain language before adding implementation detail.

concepts.title: Context
concepts.description: Explain which constraints make the technology or pattern a suitable choice.

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.description: State what complexity, cost, coupling, or operational burden the decision introduces.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.description: Use a real example, measurement, test, incident, or design decision to ground the answer.

architecture.description: A complete technical answer moves from concept to context, then trade-off and evidence instead of stopping at a definition.

code.label: AnswerFramework.cs
code.introduction: Use a compact mental model to structure an answer while keeping it conversational.

bestPractices: Answer the exact question before expanding into related knowledge.
Pair every recommendation with constraints and at least one trade-off.
Use project evidence and be honest about what you personally implemented.
Practice drawing request, data, failure, and deployment flows on a blank page.

interviewQuestions.question: How should you answer a technology-choice question?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the requirements, compare viable options against them, choose one, name the cost, and explain what evidence would validate the decision.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a strong production-readiness answer?
interviewQuestions.answer: It covers security, observability, failure handling, data recovery, deployment, capacity, ownership, and explicit gaps—not only code structure.

interviewQuestions.question: How should you respond when you do not know?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the boundary honestly, reason from what you do know, identify the risk of guessing, and explain how you would verify the answer.

note: The best interview narrative is specific enough to be credible and concise enough that the interviewer can explore it with follow-up questions.
tip: For every portfolio repository, prepare a two-minute architecture story and one concrete defect or trade-off you worked through.
warning: Do not claim production scale, security, or resilience that you only inferred from a successful build or local demo.

name: Background & Hosted Services
shortDescription: Run recurring, queued, and long-lived work outside the request path with hosted services and job schedulers.
overview: Background processing lets an application do meaningful work—emails, media pipelines, cleanup, retries—without blocking a request or depending on a client staying connected.
detail: ASP.NET Core exposes IHostedService and BackgroundService for long-lived in-process workers, while a job scheduler such as Hangfire adds persistence, retries, and visibility for fire-and-forget, delayed, recurring, and continuation jobs backed by a durable store.

concepts.title: Hosted services
concepts.description: IHostedService and BackgroundService integrate long-lived workers with the application's startup, shutdown, and dependency injection lifecycle.

concepts.title: Durable job scheduling
concepts.description: Hangfire and similar schedulers persist job state to a store so work survives restarts, deployments, and process crashes.

concepts.title: Idempotent processing
concepts.description: A retried or redelivered job must produce the same outcome as a single successful run, usually enforced with a processed-work record.

concepts.title: Claim-based concurrency
concepts.description: Database-native locking—unique constraints and a LockedUntil column—lets multiple workers pick up jobs safely without an in-app mutex.

architecture.description: A producer enqueues durable job records; one or more workers claim and process them, writing results back to the same store they were claimed from.

code.label: ExportModule.cs
code.introduction: Register a recurring job alongside its dependencies so scheduling and business logic stay in one discoverable place.

bestPractices: Make every job handler idempotent; assume at-least-once delivery and possible redelivery.
Keep job payloads small and serializable; pass identifiers, not full domain objects.
Set explicit retry limits and a dead-letter or failed-job review path instead of retrying forever.
Emit structured logs and metrics per job run so stuck or slow jobs are visible before they become an incident.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between IHostedService and a job scheduler like Hangfire?
interviewQuestions.answer: IHostedService is an in-process, code-driven worker tied to the application's own lifetime; a scheduler like Hangfire persists job state externally, so scheduling, retries, and visibility survive restarts and can be distributed across workers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does at-least-once delivery matter for background jobs?
interviewQuestions.answer: Most schedulers retry on failure or after a crash, so a handler can run more than once for the same logical job; without idempotency this can double-charge, double-send, or corrupt state.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you stop two worker instances from processing the same job?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use the job store's own concurrency control—row-level locking, a unique claim constraint, or a LockedUntil column—rather than an in-memory lock, since workers may run in separate processes or machines.

note: A hosted service and a durable job scheduler solve different problems: use the former for lightweight in-process loops and the latter when work must survive restarts or run on a schedule.
tip: Add a dashboard or admin view for scheduled and failed jobs early; debugging background work without visibility is expensive.
warning: Do not rely on in-memory queues or timers for anything that must not be lost on deploy or crash; use a durable store.
latestNote: New guide covering hosted services and durable scheduling

name: Observability & OpenTelemetry
shortDescription: Connect traces, metrics, and logs across services so production behavior is diagnosable, not guessed at.
overview: Observability means being able to ask new questions about a running system without shipping new code—usually by combining correlated traces, metrics, and structured logs.
detail: OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral way to emit traces, metrics, and logs from .NET applications. A trace follows one logical operation across service boundaries, metrics summarize behavior over time, and structured logs give point-in-time detail—together they turn an incident from guesswork into evidence.

concepts.title: Traces and spans
concepts.description: A trace represents one logical operation; spans are its timed steps, connected across process and network boundaries by a shared trace context.

concepts.title: Metrics
concepts.description: Counters, histograms, and gauges summarize behavior—request rate, latency distribution, queue depth—over time without per-event detail.

concepts.title: Correlated logs
concepts.description: Attaching trace and span identifiers to log lines lets you jump from a slow trace straight to the log lines that explain it.

concepts.title: Exporters and collectors
concepts.description: The OpenTelemetry Collector receives telemetry from applications and routes it to one or more backends without coupling code to a specific vendor.

architecture.description: Instrumented code emits traces, metrics, and logs to a collector, which routes them to a backend where they can be correlated and queried.

code.label: Telemetry.cs
code.introduction: Registering OpenTelemetry once at startup instruments ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, and EF Core without touching business code.
code.code:
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(resource => resource.AddService("orders-api"))
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddEntityFrameworkCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(metrics => metrics
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter());

bestPractices: Propagate trace context across every HTTP call, queue message, and background job, not just synchronous requests.
Instrument at the edges first—HTTP, database, messaging—before adding custom spans for business logic.
Keep high-cardinality values like user IDs on span attributes, not on metric labels, to avoid metric explosion.
Alert on symptoms users feel—latency, error rate, saturation—not only on infrastructure metrics.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does distributed tracing solve that logs alone do not?
interviewQuestions.answer: Logs are scoped to one process; a trace stitches together the spans from every service a single request touched, showing where time was actually spent across the whole call graph.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is metric cardinality a concern?
interviewQuestions.answer: Metrics backends aggregate by label combination; labels with unbounded values such as user ID or request ID can create a new time series per value and overwhelm the backend.

interviewQuestions.question: What role does the OpenTelemetry Collector play?
interviewQuestions.answer: It decouples instrumented applications from a specific observability vendor by receiving telemetry once and routing, batching, and exporting it to one or more backends.

note: Observability is a property of the system's design, not a dashboard added after an incident.
tip: Pick a small set of golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, saturation—per service and make sure they are wired end to end before adding anything fancier.
warning: Sampling every trace at high volume can be expensive and slow; use head- or tail-based sampling once traffic grows, but keep error traces at full fidelity.
latestNote: New guide on tracing, metrics, and correlated logs

name: CI/CD for .NET
shortDescription: Automate build, test, and deployment so every change is verified and shipped the same way, every time.
overview: A CI/CD pipeline turns ‘it works on my machine’ into a repeatable, observable process: restore, build, test, package, and deploy the same way for every change.
detail: Continuous integration validates every change automatically—restore, build, run tests, and check quality gates. Continuous deployment extends that pipeline to package and ship the validated artifact, ideally through progressively more production-like environments with clear rollback.

concepts.title: Pipeline stages
concepts.description: Restore, build, test, and publish run in order so a fast failure in an early stage avoids wasting time on later ones.

concepts.title: Artifacts
concepts.description: A pipeline should build one deployable artifact once and promote that same artifact through environments, not rebuild per environment.

concepts.title: Quality gates
concepts.description: Required checks—tests, coverage thresholds, static analysis, vulnerability scans—block a merge or deployment until they pass.

concepts.title: Environments and promotion
concepts.description: Separate environments with their own configuration and approval rules let a change move from validation toward production deliberately.

architecture.description: A commit triggers a pipeline that restores, builds, and tests the change, then packages and promotes one artifact through environments toward production.

code.label: .github/workflows/ci.yml
code.introduction: A focused workflow restores, builds, and tests on every pull request before anything is published.
code.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '10.0.x'
      - run: dotnet restore
      - run: dotnet build --no-restore -c Release
      - run: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --logger trx

bestPractices: Fail fast: run restore, build, and unit tests before anything slow like integration tests or container builds.
Build the deployable artifact once and reuse it across every environment instead of rebuilding per stage.
Pin tool and action versions so a pipeline behaves the same today and in six months.
Keep secrets in the platform's secret store, never in workflow files or environment variables checked into source.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Continuous delivery means every change is automatically verified and ready to release, with a manual approval to actually deploy; continuous deployment removes that manual gate and ships automatically once checks pass.

interviewQuestions.question: Why build one artifact and promote it, instead of rebuilding for each environment?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rebuilding per environment risks shipping code that differs from what was tested—different dependency versions, timestamps, or compiler output—so promoting one immutable artifact keeps what you tested and what you ship identical.

interviewQuestions.question: How should a pipeline handle a failing quality gate?
interviewQuestions.answer: It should block the merge or deployment, report the specific failure clearly, and leave the previous known-good artifact in place rather than partially deploying a change.

note: A pipeline is production code: version it, review changes to it, and test that it still does what you expect.
tip: Cache dependency restores between runs, but invalidate the cache on lockfile changes so a stale cache never hides a real dependency problem.
warning: A pipeline that deploys on green tests but has no rollback plan turns every bad merge into a production incident.
latestNote: New guide on pipeline stages and artifact promotion

name: .NET Aspire
shortDescription: Orchestrate multi-project .NET applications locally with service discovery, dashboards, and consistent configuration.
overview: .NET Aspire is an opinionated stack for building observable, cloud-native applications, giving multi-service solutions a consistent way to run, wire together, and inspect locally before they reach the cloud.
detail: An AppHost project declares the services, databases, and resources an application needs; Aspire wires up service discovery, connection strings, and telemetry automatically and starts everything together with a dashboard for logs, traces, and metrics—removing a lot of local orchestration scripts and README setup steps.

concepts.title: AppHost
concepts.description: A dedicated project declares the application's resources—APIs, databases, caches, queues—and how they depend on each other.

concepts.title: Service discovery
concepts.description: Dependent projects receive resolved endpoints for the resources they reference instead of hardcoded URLs or ports.

concepts.title: Integrations
concepts.description: Aspire components wrap common resources such as Postgres, Redis, and messaging with sensible defaults, health checks, and telemetry.

concepts.title: Dashboard
concepts.description: A local dashboard shows structured logs, traces, and metrics for every running resource without extra tooling.

architecture.description: The AppHost starts and wires together each declared resource, injecting configuration and endpoints while the dashboard observes all of them together.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: The AppHost project describes resources once; dependent projects reference them by name instead of configuring connection strings manually.

bestPractices: Keep the AppHost declarative; let it describe resources and references instead of embedding business logic.
Use the dashboard during development to check traces and logs before reaching for a debugger.
Treat local resource definitions as a starting point, not a production topology—review managed service choices separately for the cloud.
Reference resources by name through WithReference instead of hardcoding hostnames, ports, or connection strings.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does .NET Aspire solve that Docker Compose does not fully cover?
interviewQuestions.answer: It adds .NET-aware service discovery, typed resource references, and built-in OpenTelemetry wiring across projects, so dependent services and dashboards work with less manual configuration than a generic container definition.

interviewQuestions.question: Is Aspire a hosting platform?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. It is an application model and local orchestration/tooling experience; deployment still targets your chosen hosting platform, using Aspire's manifest to describe the resources needed.

interviewQuestions.question: How does a project get another resource's connection details?
interviewQuestions.answer: Through WithReference in the AppHost, which injects configuration and environment variables that the referencing project's client integration reads automatically.

note: Aspire's biggest early win is usually local development: one command starts every dependent service with wired-up configuration and a shared dashboard.
tip: Start with the AppHost even for a single API and one database; adding services later is far easier once the pattern is established.
warning: Aspire's local resource definitions are for development convenience; they are not a substitute for a real infrastructure-as-code deployment story.
latestNote: New guide on AppHost orchestration and the dashboard

name: CQRS & MediatR
shortDescription: Separate the shapes and paths used to change state from the ones used to read it, and route both through a mediator.
overview: Command Query Responsibility Segregation splits an application's write model, optimized for enforcing invariants, from its read model, optimized for the shapes a UI or report actually needs.
detail: Commands express intent to change state and return little more than an identifier or acknowledgment; queries return read-optimized projections and never mutate anything. A mediator library like MediatR routes each command or query to exactly one handler and lets cross-cutting behavior—validation, logging, transactions—wrap every request in one place.

concepts.title: Commands vs queries
concepts.description: Commands express an intent to change state and stay narrow; queries return data shaped for a specific read need and never mutate anything.

concepts.title: Single handler per request
concepts.description: Each command or query type is matched to exactly one handler, keeping request-to-behavior mapping explicit and easy to locate.

concepts.title: Pipeline behaviors
concepts.description: Cross-cutting concerns—validation, logging, transactions, authorization—wrap every request through a shared pipeline instead of being repeated per handler.

concepts.title: Read models
concepts.description: Query handlers can read from denormalized or differently shaped projections instead of the same model the write side uses.

architecture.description: A mediator routes each command or query to its handler; write handlers change the domain model while read handlers return projections shaped for their caller.

code.label: PlaceOrderCommand.cs
code.introduction: A command and its handler stay narrow, returning only what the caller needs to continue.

bestPractices: Keep command handlers focused on one business outcome; split a handler that is doing two unrelated things.
Let query handlers bypass the domain model and read directly from a projection when that projection already exists.
Put validation, logging, and transaction handling in pipeline behaviors instead of repeating them in every handler.
Version read models independently from the write model once their shapes genuinely diverge.

interviewQuestions.question: What does CQRS actually require—separate databases?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. CQRS is about separating responsibility and models for reads and writes; it can be implemented with one database and different query and command paths, and only needs physically separate stores when read and write scaling or consistency needs diverge.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem do pipeline behaviors solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: They let cross-cutting concerns like validation, logging, and transactions wrap every command or query in one place, instead of being copy-pasted into each handler.

interviewQuestions.question: When is CQRS not worth the complexity?
interviewQuestions.answer: When an application's read and write needs are simple and aligned—a single model with straightforward CRUD often serves the domain better than the extra indirection of separate command and query paths.

note: CQRS is a separation of responsibility, not automatically a separation of databases or an event-sourced write model.
tip: Introduce CQRS at the boundary where reads and writes have genuinely different shapes or scaling needs, not uniformly across every feature.
warning: Splitting commands and queries without addressing how the read side stays in sync just moves the consistency problem instead of solving it.
latestNote: New guide on commands, queries, and pipeline behaviors

name: Event-Driven Messaging
shortDescription: Coordinate independently deployed services through durable, asynchronous events instead of synchronous calls.
overview: Event-driven messaging lets services react to what happened elsewhere without a direct, blocking call, trading immediate consistency for looser coupling and better resilience to partial failure.
detail: A publisher records that something happened; a broker such as Service Bus or RabbitMQ delivers that event to one or more subscribers, each processing it independently. Because delivery can be delayed, duplicated, or reordered, the pattern's real difficulty is not publishing—it is designing durable delivery, idempotent handling, and workflows that tolerate partial completion.

concepts.title: Events vs commands
concepts.description: An event states a fact that already happened and may have many subscribers; a command requests a specific action and expects exactly one handler.

concepts.title: Transactional outbox
concepts.description: Writing a business change and its outgoing event in the same local transaction avoids the dual-write problem of updating a database and publishing separately.

concepts.title: Idempotent consumers
concepts.description: A handler records which message identifiers it has already processed so redelivery does not repeat side effects.

concepts.title: Sagas
concepts.description: A saga coordinates a multi-step workflow across services using events and compensating actions instead of a distributed transaction.

architecture.description: A service commits a business change and an outbox record in one transaction; a relay publishes the event to a broker, which delivers it to independent, idempotent subscribers.

code.label: OutboxRelay.cs
code.introduction: A background relay publishes outbox rows written in the same transaction as the business change, then marks them sent.

bestPractices: Write the outbox row in the same transaction as the business change it describes, never as a separate call.
Design every consumer to be safe against duplicate delivery before trusting the broker's delivery guarantees.
Version event contracts additively and keep old consumers working through a compatibility window.
Model multi-step workflows as explicit sagas with compensating actions instead of implicit chains of event handlers.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the dual-write problem and how does the outbox pattern fix it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dual-write happens when a service updates its database and publishes an event as two separate operations that can fail independently, leaving them out of sync; the outbox pattern writes the event as a row in the same local transaction as the business change, then relays it asynchronously, so the two are always consistent.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't most message brokers guarantee exactly-once delivery?
interviewQuestions.answer: Coordinating exactly-once delivery across a network requires distributed consensus that most brokers avoid for performance and availability reasons, so they offer at-least-once delivery and expect consumers to handle duplicates.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a saga, and why not just use a distributed transaction?
interviewQuestions.answer: A saga coordinates a multi-step process across services using a sequence of local transactions and compensating actions on failure; distributed transactions need every participant to be available and lock resources together, which does not scale or fit independently deployed services.

note: Ordering and duplication are the default in most messaging systems, not the exception; design consumers assuming both.
tip: Give every event a stable, versioned schema and a unique identifier from the start—retrofitting either is painful once consumers exist.
warning: Publishing an event before the related database transaction commits can let subscribers react to a change that gets rolled back.
latestNote: New guide on outbox delivery and idempotent consumers

name: gRPC
shortDescription: Define strongly typed service contracts and exchange compact binary messages over HTTP/2, including streaming.
overview: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to define a service contract once, generating strongly typed client and server code for fast, compact, binary communication over HTTP/2.
detail: A .proto file describes services and messages; tooling generates client stubs and server base classes so the two sides never hand-write serialization or drift on shape. Beyond simple request-response, gRPC natively supports server, client, and bidirectional streaming, making it a strong fit for internal service-to-service calls and real-time data flows.

concepts.title: Protocol Buffers
concepts.description: A compact, schema-first binary format defines message shapes once and generates typed code for multiple languages.

concepts.title: Service contracts
concepts.description: A .proto file declares RPC methods and their request/response types, acting as the single source of truth between client and server.

concepts.title: HTTP/2 transport
concepts.description: Multiplexed streams over one connection let gRPC support concurrent calls and native streaming without HTTP/1.1's per-request overhead.

concepts.title: Streaming modes
concepts.description: Server, client, and bidirectional streaming let either side send a sequence of messages over one long-lived call.

architecture.description: A shared .proto contract generates client and server code; the client calls generated stubs, and the server implements the matching generated base class.

code.label: OrderGrpcService.cs
code.introduction: A generated base class exposes strongly typed request and response messages, so the implementation stays focused on behavior.

bestPractices: Version .proto contracts additively—add new fields and methods rather than reusing or removing field numbers.
Keep gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where both ends can share the contract; expose REST or GraphQL at the public edge if broader client compatibility is needed.
Set deadlines on every call so a slow downstream service cannot hold client resources indefinitely.
Use streaming only where it fits the workload—many small independent requests are often simpler as unary calls.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is gRPC often faster than a typical JSON REST API?
interviewQuestions.answer: It uses Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format, over HTTP/2, which supports multiplexed streams on one connection—together this reduces both payload size and connection overhead compared to text-based JSON over HTTP/1.1.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose REST over gRPC?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the API needs to be broadly consumable by browsers and third parties without generated clients, or when human-readable payloads and simple tooling matter more than raw performance.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the three streaming modes gRPC supports beyond unary calls?
interviewQuestions.answer: Server streaming, where the server sends multiple responses to one request; client streaming, where the client sends multiple requests for one response; and bidirectional streaming, where both sides send messages independently over the same call.

note: A .proto file is a contract between teams as much as a code-generation input; treat changes to it with the same care as a public API.
tip: Generate client and server code as part of the build so the contract and the implementation can never silently drift apart.
warning: Browsers cannot call raw gRPC directly; use grpc-web or a gateway if browser clients need to reach a gRPC service.
latestNote: New guide on contracts, HTTP/2, and streaming modes

name: SignalR
shortDescription: Push real-time updates from server to client over WebSockets, with automatic fallback and connection management.
overview: SignalR lets a server push messages to connected clients as events happen, instead of clients repeatedly polling for changes.
detail: A hub is a strongly typed entry point both sides can call methods on. SignalR negotiates the best available transport—WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or long polling—and manages reconnection, while groups let the server target subsets of connected clients such as one user's devices or one tenant's dashboard viewers.

concepts.title: Hubs
concepts.description: A hub is a server-side class clients connect to and call methods on; the server can call back to connected clients through the same hub.

concepts.title: Transport negotiation
concepts.description: SignalR automatically selects WebSockets when available and falls back to other transports, so application code does not manage the transport directly.

concepts.title: Groups and users
concepts.description: Connections can be organized into groups or targeted by user identifier, letting the server send updates to exactly the right audience.

concepts.title: Backplane
concepts.description: A backplane such as Redis fans messages out across multiple server instances so clients connected to different servers still receive the same broadcasts.

architecture.description: Clients connect to a hub over a negotiated transport; the server calls back to individual connections, groups, or all clients as events occur.

code.label: OrderStatusHub.cs
code.introduction: A hub method adds a caller to a group; a separate service call notifies just that group when an order's status changes.

bestPractices: Scope broadcasts to groups instead of sending to all clients, so unrelated connections don't receive irrelevant traffic.
Add a backplane before scaling to multiple server instances, or clients on different instances will miss messages.
Design the client for reconnection—buffer or re-fetch state on reconnect instead of assuming no messages were missed.
Keep hub methods thin; delegate business logic to application services the same way an API controller would.

interviewQuestions.question: How does SignalR decide which transport to use?
interviewQuestions.answer: It negotiates with the client and prefers WebSockets when both the browser and any intermediate proxies support it, falling back to Server-Sent Events or long polling otherwise, without the application needing to choose a transport explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a backplane needed when scaling SignalR horizontally?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each server instance only knows about the connections it holds directly; a backplane like Redis relays messages between instances so a broadcast reaches clients connected anywhere, not just on the server that triggered it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a SignalR group used for?
